t: Oligarchy, Greek for “rule by few”, named the many Greek constitutions that kept power with the propertied; Aristotle called it a corrupt form of government, rule by the rich for the rich.
The Republic of Venice, whose Great Council was closed to new families from 1297, was the longest-lived oligarchy, governed by a hereditary patriciate until its fall in 1797.
Today the word is used loosely for the political power of great wealth, and Robert Michels’s “iron law of oligarchy” of 1911 held that all large organisations, even democratic ones, fall to a few.
dyk: From 1268 Venice elected its doge in ten rounds that alternated drawing lots with voting, from thirty members of the Great Council drawn by lot to forty-one electors, to defeat bribery and family factions.
ev: Athens begins its yearly list of archons, an office then reserved for the well-born families, the Eupatridae
In Herodotus’s Histories the Persian Megabyzus makes the first recorded case for rule by a few of the best men
The oligarchic Four Hundred overthrow the Athenian democracy, which is restored within a year
Sparta installs the Thirty at Athens; in eight months they kill about 1,500 citizens before democracy returns
Aristotle’s Politics defines oligarchy as government by the wealthy in their own interest
The Serrata begins to close Venice’s Great Council to new families, creating a hereditary ruling patriciate
Venice’s Council of Ten has Doge Marino Faliero beheaded for plotting to make himself lord of the city
Facing Napoleon’s ultimatum, Venice’s Great Council votes the Republic out of existence on 12 May

f.power: A small group defined by wealth or birth, which alone holds the councils, magistracies and votes
f.legitimacy: Property, birth or entry in a closed register, defended as the stake and competence of those with most to lose; the laws were made by and for the few
f.chosen: Members elect or co-opt one another into councils and short-term offices; property qualifications or hereditary lists such as Venice’s Golden Book keep others out
f.examples: Corinth under the Bacchiadae, Athens under the Four Hundred and the Thirty, Florence under the Albizzi, the Republic of Venice, the Republic of Genoa
